The working folder a run is admitted to (P1.5) and started in.

Identity is a [`ProjectId`] rather than a path: the project already
carries a canonical root the host validates at launch, and an id is what a
second device can *name* without being able to resolve it (D15, D16). The
folder inside it is text a person chose, and is redacted like every path.

**`None` is unreachable at admission.** It exists so a request can be
built before a scope is chosen and so the modal has a state to refuse;
P1.5 makes it impossible to start a run with it. M4 adds git shapes —
a worktree per run — as new variants, which is why this is an enum.

RelativeFolder.description:
A folder inside a working scope's root, as a person typed or chose
it. A path is private (standing requirement 7); the host canonicalizes
it at admission and this type only bounds and hides it.

oneOf.description: A whole document at one captured version.

One block of a document, at one captured version of that document.
The version is the document's — a block has no history of its own.

A file, image or PDF from the content-addressed blob store, pinned at
its hash. Retention is asserted at capture (§7.2 step 2).

RunContextItem.description:
One item of context, pinned.

The workspace travels with every item because content lives in exactly
one workspace and a document id alone cannot say which room to open
(DATAMODEL, *content lives in exactly one workspace*).

BlobKind.description:
What kind of bytes a blob item carries. The kind decides how the item is
materialized for the provider (P1.7); the hash decides what it is.

CreateRunResponse.description: `202 Accepted`: the request is durable and the run exists.

oneOf.description: The Run document exists; nothing has been asked to start.
Admission, materialization and session creation are under way.

The provider is up. `attention` and `control` are the markers §7.5
and §7.4 put on a running run instead of more states; both default so
a header written before either existed still reads.
A restart ended the attempt (D10). Never `Failed`; offers Resume.
An orchestrator turn completed the objective with nothing pending.
Minted for M5 (UC14); no transition reaches it in M1.
Minted for M5 (UC13); no transition reaches it in M1.

RunStatus.description:
Where a run is. One canonical authority — the Run document — holds it
(§7.1); `runs.db` never carries a second one.

AttentionSet.description: The attention markers on a `Running` run. Sorted and duplicate-free.

oneOf.description:
The provider asked for an approval. M1 answers it through the
existing session controls (D29).
The provider is waiting for input. Not terminal (§7.5).

The provider spawned a child session, which §7.3 terminates. The
marker stays until the termination is observed.

An orchestrator turn ended having registered no artifact: finished
and needing attention, never a delivered result (D29).

Attention.description:
Something a `Running` run wants a person to look at. A set, because an
approval and a detected child session can both be outstanding.

oneOf.description: The orchestrator submits turns.

A person asked for control; the request waits for the turn boundary,
and the orchestrator submits nothing more until control returns.

A person holds the lease. Automatic submission is fenced; observation
stays live.

ControlState.description:
Who holds the session's controller while a run is `Running` (§7.4).

`objective_satisfied` is the fence: an orchestrator turn that completed
the objective while a handover was pending does not end the run — the
handover it was about to yield to wins — and the fact is carried here so
that when control returns the run completes without a second turn.

oneOf.description:
Nothing survived — the host restarted, or the session is known to
have ended. A fresh attempt is safe.

No evidence on a host that did not restart: nothing is running and
nothing can start under the retired key, but earlier work may exist.
Never auto-resumed; a person decides.

PriorAttempt.description: What recovery could prove about the attempt a restart interrupted (§7.6).

oneOf.description: The scope could not be admitted (P1.5).
A context item could not be captured (§7.2 step 2).
A captured item could not be materialized (§7.2 step 3).
The provider session could not be created.
The provider process did not start.

The run's authority record or MCP endpoint could not be established
(§7.3).
The provider reported the turn failed.

FailureStage.description:
Why a start or a turn failed. A closed vocabulary — a stage, never a
message — so a failure can be reported anywhere without carrying text.

sessions.description:
The provider session each listed run is being driven in **on the
device that answered**, for the runs where there is one.

The same fact [`RunExecution::session`] carries about a single run,
and deliberately not a header field for the same reason: a header is
what a run means on every device, and which session is driving it
*here* is execution state (D3, D15). The listing carries it so a
surface that draws every run — the Agents navigator — can put a run's
session underneath the run without one `GET /v1/runs/{run}` per row.

Absent for a run between attempts, for a run that has ended, and for
every run another device is executing. `#[serde(default)]`, so a
listing from a worker that predates the field reads as *no session
known* rather than failing to decode.

documents.description:
**The Run document each listed run is registered as.**

A run is a document in the workspace's manifest, and deleting one is
that document going into the workspace's bin like every other
document in Koru — which is a manifest edit, and the manifest belongs
to the window rather than to this worker. So the listing says which
document each run is, and the window that asks for a run to be
deleted has the id it needs to move it.

`#[serde(default)]`, so a listing from a worker that predates the
field reads as *no documents named* rather than failing to decode.

trashed.description:
**The runs of this workspace that are in the trash**, newest
deletion first. Absent from `runs`: a trashed run is not a run you
are looking at any more, and the Agents navigator stops listing it
the moment it goes.

requested_model.description:
The person's explicit choice; absent means the provider default.
Retained intent, never proof of the model the provider actually used.

context.description:
Context as given — pinned, and unchanged by anything that happens to
the source afterwards (§7.2).

grants.description: The grant set (D28). A resume re-reads it and never widens it.

failure_reason.description: Safe terminal cause, absent for older runs. Raw provider text is never retained here.

artifacts.description: Every result registered, in registration order.

economics.description:
A projection of the retained usage facts and the timeline (§17.1),
recomputable; kept here so a device reads the numbers without
replaying.

origin.description:
Durable provenance copied from the creation intent. Additive and
defaulted so runs written before scheduling remain manual.

oneOf.description:
A device of the person's own, named so every other device can say
which one is running the work (D16).

ExecutionEnvironment.description:
The machine a run executes on (D3: execution machinery is device-local).

One variant today. D12 makes the orchestrator cloud-deployable later, and
that arrives as a second variant here rather than as a flag on the device
— which is why this is `#[non_exhaustive]`: a dependant that matches it
must already say what it does with an environment it does not know.

ResultReference.description:
A result, named (D27).

The fields a device that cannot open the bytes still shows: what it is,
how big, when, and which device holds it. Opening begins working when
replication ships (M7); until then a second device reads this and says
the content is elsewhere.

orchestrator_turns.description: Turns the timeline recorded, by originator.

turns_with_usage.description: Turns with a usage fact, after replay.

elapsed_ms.description:
§17.2: wall-clock excluding time spent `Interrupted` or under human
control. `None` until the run has started.

models.description: Every model any turn used, as references.

complete.description:
Whether every usage fact was complete. A single incomplete fact makes
the summary incomplete, because a price over it would be a guess.

EconomicsSummary.description:
The run's economics as the header carries them (D39): a projection of
the replayed facts and the timeline, recomputable at any time.

TokenTotal.description:
A token total that knows what it is missing. `known` sums every turn
that reported; `unavailable_turns` counts every turn that did not, so a
surface renders "at least 1,200 (2 turns unreported)" rather than
"1,200" — or "unavailable" when nothing reported at all.

RunRating.description:
A rating as recorded: the gesture, the optional note, who and when.

The note lives here — in the run's own content — and nowhere else (D44).
`delegate.run.rated` carries the rating and the ids; a metric carries the
rating; neither ever carries the note.

Rating.description:
One gesture on a finished run (D44): good or not good. An unrated run is
a normal state, which is why the header holds an `Option<RunRating>` and
this enum has no "unrated" arm.

RatingNote.description:
The optional note beside a rating (D44). It lives in the run's own
content and never in an event attribute or a metric, so a private
remark cannot become a free-text analytics field.

RunOrigin.description:
Where a run came from. The scheduled form is derived from the consumed
schedule authority and retained in the creation intent, so recovery cannot
turn an unattended firing into a manual start.

document.description: The Run document, so the window can restore or purge it.

trashed_at_ms.description:
When it was put in the trash, as the manifest recorded it. `None`
for a manifest entry that carries no timestamp — an older client
wrote it — and the row then sorts to the bottom rather than claiming
a moment nobody recorded.

artifacts.description:
What the person said should happen to its results. `Keep` for a run
nobody was asked about, which is every run that produced nothing.

TrashedRun.description: One run in the trash, as the Trash tab draws it.

oneOf.description:
The results stay in the Artifacts column with their provenance
intact. That provenance names a run that no longer exists, and the
Artifact Store records the deletion so the sentence says the run was
deleted rather than printing an id nothing resolves.

The results go with the run: every family the run created is
retired. Their versions stay — a version is immutable and the store
retires rather than erases — but the column stops offering them.

ArtifactDisposition.description:
**What a person said should happen to a deleted run's results.**

A run that produced nothing is never asked. A run that did is, once,
when it goes into the trash — and the answer waits there with it, because
trashing changes nothing in the artifact store and emptying the trash is
what acts.

**Keep is the default and the safe one.** A run with no answer recorded
keeps what it produced: a build that predates the question, a recording
that was lost, a run that arrived by sync. Nothing infers *delete*.

context.description:
What each of the header's context pins points at *now* (D46, D47),
in the header's own order. Either empty — this device could not
resolve the sources, and a surface says nothing rather than saying
"gone" — or exactly as long as `header.context`.

RunView.description:
`GET /v1/runs/{run}`: the header, what this device holds, the state of
each pinned source, and a window of the history.

session.description:
The provider session of the attempt this device is driving right
now. `None` everywhere else — on another device, between attempts,
and after the run ended — and a surface offers no handover without
it.

run_workspace.description:
**The folder the agent is working in**, as this device resolved it.
A scope says what *kind* of folder was asked for — a project's root,
a folder inside one, or one Koru makes — and only the device driving
the run knows which one that turned out to be. A person judging a run
they did not watch is entitled to be told where it happened.

`None` on a device that is not driving it, and before an attempt has
one. It is a path, so it is a person's own and stays on this wire: it
reaches no log, no event attribute and no metric (§13.7).

RunExecution.description:
What the device that answered can do about the run, and what it holds
(D3, D15, §7.4).

Deliberately **not** a header field: the header is what a run means on
every device, and how far *this* machine got is execution state. A
surface compares [`Self::device`] with the header's executing device to
decide whether it may offer an action at all, and takes control through
[`Self::session`] when there is one.

oneOf.description: Listed, not in the trash, and the pinned bytes are retained.

In the workspace's trash — its own stamp or an ancestor's. The
pinned bytes are still retained; restore makes it live again.

The pinned bytes cannot be opened here: the document was purged
(its versions cascade with it), the blob is gone, or the workspace
is.

ContextState.description: The current state of a pinned source. The pin itself never changes.

TimelineItem.description:
One entry of the history as the wire carries it. `Unrecognized` is an
entry this build could not decode, in its place.

oneOf.description: The Run document was committed (§7.1 step 3).
An attempt's provider is up.

`ToolCompleted` events, coalesced (§7.5: bounded, never one row per
call).

**`failures` is what makes the count actionable** — which tools
failed and how, in tokens, bounded by type. An entry written before
this build carries none, and reads as the counts alone: the same
sentence it has always drawn, with nothing invented under it.
Rejection is news (§7.5).
A child session appeared and was terminated (§7.3).
A restart ended the attempt (§7.6).

The human lease was granted. `discovered` marks a takeover recovery
found already in place, timestamped at discovery (§7.4).

Facts Koru never received — a provider tail evicted during delegate
downtime. `events_lost` when the eviction reported a count.

A manual start proceeded onto a folder another run holds (D34,
§7.8): the warning the person saw and overrode, as a step. `holders`
counts the runs that held it; their attempts ride the refs.

StepKind.description:
What a step is. A closed enum mirroring §7.5's rows plus control
handover (§7.4), artifact registration, recovery and the honest gap
(§7.1: replay never invents what it did not receive). Counts ride the
variant that needs them, bounded by type.

oneOf.description: The delegate worker, pursuing the objective.
A person who took control of the session (§7.4).

StoredToolFailures.description:
How the breakdown is written down: the listed pairs and the tail's
count, both absent when there are none. A fixed array would store eight
nulls in every entry; this stores nothing in the ordinary case.

calls.description:
How many calls of this tool failed this way. Never zero in a listed
tally.

Sixteen bits, because a coalesced step is written at the turn's end
or at the orchestrator's tool bound, whichever comes first — no one
step has ever counted more than a couple of hundred calls, and a
count that somehow did would saturate rather than wrap.

ToolFailureTally.description:
One tool, one way it failed, and how many times that happened in the
turn.

oneOf.description: Running a command.
Editing files.
A tool an MCP server offers.
A tool the provider loaded at runtime.

A tool this build has no token for. The honest answer when an
adapter — or an older peer that sent no kind at all — did not say.

ToolKind.description:
**Which tool ran**, as the adapter that watched it declares.

Not the provider's name for it: an adapter maps its provider's own tool
vocabulary onto this list, and a tool it has no token for is
[`Other`](Self::Other) — named as unknown rather than passed through as
text.

oneOf.description: It was not allowed to run — an approval refused, a permission denied.
It was stopped before it finished.
It ran out of time.
It ran and reported an error.

It did not succeed, and the provider did not say why in a way this
adapter can place.

ToolFailure.description:
**Why a tool call did not work**, classified by the adapter from the
structured fields it already reads.

Five classes and no sixth escape hatch that carries text. A provider
that failed a call in a way the adapter cannot place is
[`Unclassified`](Self::Unclassified) — which is a fact worth showing
("it failed, and the provider did not say how") and is never a guess.

oneOf.description: The person ended the job. The run is `Cancelled`.

The person ended the *step* to take control immediately (§7.4). The
run stays `Running`; the handover proceeds.

CancelReason.description: Why a turn was cancelled (D36). **Only `Run` terminalizes.**

oneOf.description: The adapter's own resume token continued the provider session.

The objective was re-submitted with the original pins and the
artifacts so far — a fresh attempt, not continuity.

ResumeSeam.description: Which seam a resume went through (P1.9: the timeline says which).

TimelineRefs.description: The references of one step, bounded by [`MAX_TIMELINE_REFS`].

oneOf.description:
A document as the run received it — the pin, so a later deletion is
rendered as the target's state (D46), never as a missing step.

The schedule authority that created this run. The claimed revision and
occurrence ride with it so a later template edit cannot rewrite history.

TimelineRef.description: Something a step touched, by id.

at_ms.description:
Epoch milliseconds UTC, for display and for the §17.2 definitions.
Order is the timeline's own — append order — never this clock.

TimelineEntry.description: One step of a run's history (D45).

AmendmentRevision.description:
The monotonic amendment revision of a usage fact. A retry repeats it; a
correction raises it.

oneOf.description:
The provider's note does not say whether `input` includes cached
input, so neither can be trusted alone.

The turn used more than one model and the provider gave no
attributable slices.

The provider reported no usage for the turn at all; the observable
metrics still count.

IncompleteReason.description:
Why a usage fact is incomplete. Recorded rather than guessed, because a
wrong assumption here misprices every run silently (§17.2).

identity.description: Stable across retries and amendments alike.

input.description: `None` is unavailable. It is never zero for missing.

UsageFact.description:
One turn's usage, as a durable typed fact (§17.1: committed in the run's
own storage before it is published). Ids, counts and a reference — it
copies nothing (§17.2a).

CancelRunResponse.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/cancel`: the header after the cancellation was
asked for. During a turn the run is still `Running` until the provider
answers; the stream carries the end.

ResumeRunRequest.description:
`POST /v2/runs/{run}/resume`. The body is optional and every field
defaults, so a resume of an ordinary interruption is a bodyless POST.

`confirm` is **a person deciding, never evidence**. §7.6's last row —
no evidence from a host that did not restart — proves that nothing is
running and nothing can start under the retired key, and leaves earlier
work possibly done and unobserved. Such a run is never resumed on its
own; a person is told that and asks for it deliberately, which is what
this flag carries. It changes nothing about the fence: the key is
retired at the host before the next generation opens either way, and a
key found live still refuses with `attempt_live`. Ignored for a run
whose prior attempt is known to have ended.

ResumeRunResponse.description: `POST /v2/runs/{run}/resume`: the header after the fresh attempt began.

RateRunRequest.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/rate`: one gesture on a finished run (D44).

The note travels here because it lives in the run's own content and
nowhere else — never an event attribute, never a metric. The event the
worker publishes carries the rating and whether a note exists, and not
a byte of the note itself.

TrashRunRequest.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/trash`: the run is going into the trash, and this
is the answer to the one question the trash asks about its results.

The body is optional and its one field defaults, so trashing a run that
produced nothing is a bodyless POST.

TrashRunResponse.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/trash`: the header, and the document the caller now
has to move into the workspace's bin.

**The worker records; the window moves.** Trashing a run is a manifest
edit and the manifest is the window's, so this call is the half only the
worker can do — refusing a run that is still working, and remembering
what to do with its results — and it answers with what the other half
needs.

RestoreRunResponse.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/restore`: the run is coming back out of the trash,
whole. Nothing was deleted, so there is nothing to undo — the decision
about its results is forgotten and the document is the caller's to move
back.

artifacts_retired.description:
How many result families were retired because the person asked for
them to go with the run. Zero when they asked to keep them, and for
a run that produced nothing.

PurgeRunResponse.description:
`POST /v1/runs/{run}/purge`: **the trash was emptied, and this run is
gone.**

Everything this device holds about it: the ledger's rows, its authority
record, and its working folder **when Koru made that folder**. A run
scoped to a project ran inside the person's own repository, and that
directory was theirs before the run and is theirs after — `folder` says
which of those happened, because a trash that quietly did less than it
offered teaches somebody that it did more.

The Run document is not purged here: it is a document of the workspace's
manifest, and the caller removes it once this has answered. Ordered that
way deliberately — a folder the filesystem refuses is
`run_folder_not_removed` with nothing changed, so the run stays in the
trash and can be deleted again.

oneOf.description: Koru made it, and it is gone.

**The person's own project folder, left alone.** Not silence: this
is what the trash tells them it did.

Koru made it and it was not there — an earlier delete, a tidied
temporary directory, a machine that lost it.

FolderOutcome.description:
**What emptying the trash did to a run's working folder.**

The trash says what it did, because an operation that quietly does less
than it offered teaches a person that it did more. Three answers, and
the middle one is the important one: a run scoped to a project ran
inside a folder that was the person's before it started and is theirs
after, so the run is forgotten and the directory is left exactly alone.

A folder the filesystem refused to remove is not here: that refuses the
whole deletion, so the run stays in the trash and can be deleted again.

oneOf.description:
The worker stopped streaming — the run ended, or the worker is
going away. A client resumes with `after` set to the last index.

RunStreamItem.description:
`GET /v1/runs/{run}/stream?after=…`, one SSE event each: a history
entry with its index, a status change, or the end of the stream.

name.description:
Defaultable for the earlier unreleased v5 response shape. A missing
value is displayed with the objective-derived compatibility fallback.

ScheduleView.description:
One canonical schedule projection. `header` is the stored authored value;
`state` is the converged ownership/lifecycle reduction.

ScheduleName.description:
A person-authored schedule label. It is presentation metadata, never
schedule identity, and is redacted anywhere a derived `Debug` can reach.

effective_at_ms.description:
The inclusive lower bound for occurrences under this revision. Edits
and resumes advance it, so a new rule cannot catch up older slots.

ScheduleDefinition.description:
One coherent definition edit. The document boundary rejects revision 0
and any edit that does not advance exactly once.

DelegationTemplate.description:
The reusable request fields. `RunId`, executing device, and document
version pins exist only for one claimed firing and cannot be stored here.

ScheduleContextPointer.description:
A live pointer selected for every future firing. This deliberately cannot
be placed in a [`koru_delegate_core::DelegationRequest`], which requires pinned bytes.

RecurrenceRule.description:
A persisted recurrence rule. The variants preserve Koru's existing
floating-versus-zoned distinction without an optional timezone.

CronExpression.description: A canonical expression in Koru's bounded five-field cron dialect.

SchedulePauseReason.description: A content-free reason a schedule is ineligible to fire.

ScheduleContextFailureStage.description: The context operation that made a future firing unsafe.

ScheduleNextFiring.description:
What a schedule list can truthfully say about its next occurrence.
A floating rule owned by another device has no exact instant here because
the schedule schema deliberately stores no owner timezone.

ScheduleFiringView.description:
One schedule firing as a surface may consume it. The schedule ledger mints
a planned RunId for every claim, including skips, but only a `fired` claim
denotes a Run. Skipped planned ids therefore never cross this boundary.

ScheduleFiringOutcome.description: The immutable outcome of one schedule occurrence.

CreateScheduleRequest.description:
`POST /v1/schedules`. The client mints the stable schedule identity and
supplies only reusable intent. The worker stamps owner, revision,
lifecycle, creation time, and revision-effective time.

incomplete.description:
At least one schedule-shaped Store entry could not be read while this
projection was made. Healthy rows remain useful and visible; callers
must not present this response as a complete inventory when true.

ScheduleChange.description:
Opaque, content-free invalidation for a schedule list. `instance` changes
across worker restarts so a client never mistakes a reset counter for an
already-observed generation.

ContentEncoding.description: How `read` spells the bytes it returns.

oneOf.description: The bytes were valid UTF-8 and `content` is the text itself.
`content` is the bytes, base64 (standard alphabet, padded).

GlobalSettings.description: Everything that applies to Koru as a whole, whoever is consuming it.

global_dictation_enabled.description:
Whether Agent may open a global microphone session and insert into an
external application. Off until the person accepts the Voice notice.
`None` means the first-use notice has never been accepted; `Some`
remembers onboarding independently of the current enabled value.

global_dictation_shortcut.description:
The person's preferred global Dictation chord. Agent reports the
registered fallback separately; this is intent, not availability.

delegate_temporary_root.description:
**Where Koru makes a folder for a delegated run that belongs to no
project** (ADR-365). `None` means the platform's temporary directory —
`%TMP%` on Windows, `/tmp` on Unix — which is
[`crate::paths::delegate_temporary_base`]'s answer and the only place
the default is spelled.

Device-local because it names a directory on *this* machine: the same
person's other computer has different disks, and a path that travelled
would send a run to a folder that is not there.

A string rather than a `PathBuf` because it crosses JSON and the wire,
and because an unreadable value has to survive a round trip rather than
fail a load — the consumer falls back to the default instead.

recording.description: The internal session recorder's prefill. Device-local — see the type.

ThemeChoice.description:
`theme=` in `preferences.conf`, and the terminal row's `theme=`.

Matches `koru_draw::theme::ThemePreference`: case-sensitive, because
that is what the existing parser does and a file written in another
case has never been produced by any build.

CaretWidthChoice.description:
`caret_width=`.

`x4`/`x8` are accepted on read and never written — an asymmetry
inherited from `koru_draw::theme::CaretWidth::parse`, kept because
files carrying them exist.

oneOf.description: Use whatever this build's default for the role is, now and later.
Use this family, whatever the build's default becomes.

FontSetting.description:
What a font role is set to.

**"Follow the app default" is a state, not a value.** The alternative —
writing today's default into the file — froze the default forever: v1 files
wrote every font key on every save, and nobody saw a new default font until
their file was deleted. So `FollowDefault` persists as *no key at all*, and
a chosen family is always written even when it happens to equal the current
default. That last part is a deliberate change from the pre-SP-6 writer,
which omitted a key whose value matched the default and so could not tell
a choice from a habit either.

FontFamily.description:
The typeface a font role names.

The tokens and their order are `koru_draw::theme::FontChoice`'s; the
order is load-bearing there (role globals store an index) and is kept
identical here so the two cannot drift into disagreeing about it.

Zoom.description:
A zoom factor, valid only within the range the app has always accepted.

Out of range is *ignored* rather than clamped — the guarded-geometry
stance: a file carrying nonsense keeps the default rather than snapping to
a surprising value the person never chose.

ViewModeChoice.description:
`view_mode=` — the default view mode for a newly opened document.

Unknown input becomes `Full`, matching `parse_view_mode`.

CanvasBackground.description:
The canvas background a new document opens with.

`Auto` persists as the literal `auto`; a color persists as `#rrggbb` in
lowercase. Alpha is not stored and is always opaque, exactly as today.

DictationGesture.description:
`dictation_toggle=` as a named gesture rather than a bare flag.

**The disk spelling and the API spelling are deliberately different.** On
disk it is `0`/`1`, because that is the byte already written in every
`preferences.conf` and three parsers read it. Over the API it is
`push_to_talk`/`toggle`, because `"dictation_gesture": "1"` is a riddle at
the call site — and the two parsers that read `dictation_toggle` disagree
about `true` (one accepts it, one does not), which is exactly the kind of
question a typed value should stop anybody having to ask.

LanguageChoice.description:
A language preference: automatic, or one BCP 47 tag.

The authority validates the *shape* of a tag and never resolves it: the
closed set of languages lives with each consumer (`koru-i18n` for the UI,
the speech engine for dictation, the spell engine for spelling), and
pinning a copy of any of them here would be a second list to keep true.
An unrecognized tag resolves to automatic at the consumer.

Grew out of the dictation preference when spell checking needed exactly
the same shape; [`DictationLanguage`] remains as an alias so nothing
renames on the wire or at a call site.

DictationInput.description:
Which microphone dictation opens.

The device *name* roams with the person rather than staying on the machine
— ADR-252's recorded reasoning, kept deliberately.

GlobalShortcut.description:
The chord that raises global search.

Currently writerless — no surface changes it — but the registry defines it
anyway, because a setting the app reads and nothing can write is exactly
the hole this authority exists to close.

DictationShortcut.description: A global Dictation chord accepted by Agent's single hotkey pump.

preset.description:
The preset token — `current`, `youtube`, `tiktok`, `square`,
`portrait`, `web`, `custom`. Empty means first use: *Current window
size*, which is the modal's own default.

custom_width.description:
The last custom pair typed, kept whatever preset was chosen so
*Custom…* never opens empty.

frame_rate.description: 60 or 30. `None` is first use — 60, the modal's default.

cursor.description: Whether the mouse cursor is in the clip. `None` is first use — on.

folder.description: The folder the last clip went to. `None` asks for the Videos folder.

RecordingPrefs.description:
The session recorder's last-used modal values (SESSIONRECORD) — an
internal dev tool's prefill and nothing more.

Device-local like [`GlobalSettings::delegate_temporary_root`]: the folder
names a directory on *this* machine, and the rest travels with it because
a recording rig is a machine, not a person. Written whole — the modal
always settles the set at once — and read tolerantly: a value this build
does not understand degrades to the default, never to a failed load.

TerminalSettings.description:
Koru Terminal's appearance.

**Roaming**, which is a change: these lived in this machine's `windows.conf`
row, beside the geometry, purely because the terminal had one file. How a
terminal looks is a preference about the person, not about the monitor it
happened to be opened on.

font.description:
Mono-restricted, and deliberately **not** Global's `code_font`: a code
block in a document and a terminal grid are different surfaces, and
somebody who wants a wide face for one rarely wants it for the other.

composer_default.description:
Whether a *new* window opens with its composer showing.

The default only. Whether the composer is open in a window that already
exists is furniture, and stays that window's `input_area` row.

TerminalCursorWidth.description:
The terminal row's `cursor_width=`.

`application` means "follow the app's caret width" — the terminal's own
spelling of a follow state, and unrelated to the four font settings.

AiSettings.description:
The AI section — **a facade, not a store.**

The values live in `ai.db` behind the AI worker, and the secrets live in
the OS vault behind `koru-ai-provider`. Both authorities are unchanged.
This type is the shape the facade presents; the mapping onto the worker is
the Gateway's, because the worker handle is the Gateway's.

**A secret never appears here, in either direction.** The only thing said
about the OpenAI key is whether one is configured.

AiProvider.description: Which AI provider is selected. The closed set `ai.db`'s CHECK allows.

credential_configured.description: Whether a key is in the vault. **Read-only, and never a value.**

GlobalPatch.description: One patch of [`GlobalSettings`]. Absent fields are left alone.

delegate_temporary_root.description:
`null` puts it back to the platform's temporary directory, which is
why this is a [`Field`] and not an `Option`: *absent*, *null* and *a
path* are three different instructions and only two of them fit in an
`Option`.

recording.description:
The recorder's prefill, written whole on every *Record*. Absent
leaves the stored set alone.

AiPatch.description:
One patch of [`AiSettings`].

The nullable fields use [`Field`] so that clearing a model is expressible:
`"openai_model": null` clears it, and omitting the key leaves it alone.

WorkspaceLifecycleRequest.description:
The one destructive workspace operation's body.

**The consequence is presented by the caller and accepted before this is
sent** (rev 4 §4.2 step 2, S13). What crosses is the acceptance: the token
the gateway issued alongside the consequence it computed, round-tripped
unchanged — see [`WorkspaceConfirmation`].

It is still not a credential: the scope is what authorizes the operation.
What the token adds is that the acceptance is *about* something. A token
the gateway does not recognise, one issued for another workspace or another
action, one already spent, or one that has expired is refused before
anything is closed.

oneOf.description: Hide the workspace and its projects. Reversible; its terminals close.

Move the workspace to the trash. Recoverable until the retention window
purges it; its terminals close.

Bring a soft-deleted workspace back. Closes nothing — its projects
reappear with no project mutation.

WorkspaceLifecycleAction.description:
What `POST /v1/workspaces/{id}/lifecycle` is being asked to do.

**Three verbs, and no permanent delete.** There is no purge route anywhere
in Koru — the retention sweep is the only thing that removes bytes — so
naming one here would be describing an operation that does not exist.

terminated_sessions.description:
The sessions this call closed. Empty on a retry, and empty for
`restore`, which closes nothing.

sessions_closed.description: Whether step 3 completed. `false` means nothing after it was attempted.

mutation_applied.description:
Whether step 4 committed. `false` with `sessions_closed: true` is
exactly S24, and the retry is the same request again.

WorkspaceLifecycleOutcome.description:
What the operation actually did, in the order it did it.

**Every field is a fact about this call, and the shape is the same whether
it succeeded.** S24 is a partial failure — the terminals are closed and the
catalog is unchanged — and a caller that has to report that truth needs the
same body it would have read on success, not a bare error string.

WorkspaceConfirmationRequest.description:
What `POST /v1/workspaces/{id}/lifecycle/confirmation` is being asked
about.

The dialog asks before it draws anything, because what it draws is the
answer: which terminals this action would close.

sessions.description:
The terminals this action would close, in the order the operation
would close them. Empty for `restore`, which closes nothing.

expires_at.description:
When this token stops being accepted, in epoch milliseconds. A dialog
left open past it asks again rather than sending something stale.

WorkspaceConfirmation.description:
**A consequence the gateway computed, and the token that proves it was
shown.**

The caller presents `sessions` (S13), and if the person accepts it sends
`confirmation` straight back in a [`WorkspaceLifecycleRequest`]. The token
is bound to this workspace, this action and this list, and it is spent by
being used — so an acceptance is provably about the consequence that was on
screen rather than one the caller says it displayed. ADR-267 recorded this
as the recommendation; SP-8b's dialog is the round trip it was waiting for.

**It is still not a credential.** `workspace.destroy` is what authorizes the
operation; this only says which question was answered. A token nobody can
guess is not the point — a caller holding the scope could always mint its
own before — the point is that the gateway and the dialog agree about what
was accepted.

WorkspaceSessionConsequence.description:
One terminal a confirmation names, in the words the dialog shows.

**Enough to recognise a terminal and nothing more.** A person deciding
whether to archive a workspace needs to know which windows are about to
close, which is a name and where it is working; the process state, the
controller, the attention counters and the capability set are the session
surface's business and would only make this list harder to read.

WorkspaceMigrationConfirmationRequest.description:
What `POST /v1/workspaces/{id}/migration/confirmation` is being asked about.

**The destination, and not the origin.** The gateway reads the origin from
the catalog; a caller that named it could name a stale one, and a token
bound to the wrong pair would refuse a move that is perfectly fine.

to.description: The profile the workspace would move to.

from.description: The profile that owns it now.

to.description: The profile it would move to.

sessions.description:
The terminals the move would close, in the order it would close them.
Empty when the workspace is already owned by `to` — a move that has
nothing to do closes nothing.

WorkspaceMigration.description:
**A move's consequence, and the token that proves it was shown.**

The same contract as [`WorkspaceConfirmation`], for a different question.
The token is bound to this workspace *and this destination*: a person shown
"these four terminals will close, and Notes goes to Home" has not accepted
anything about a move to some other profile, and a dialog that could
round-trip one token into a different destination would make the acceptance
meaningless.

`from` is here because the dialog names both ends of the move, and reading
it off the catalog separately would be a second chance to be out of date in
a different way than the operation is.

WorkspaceMigrationRequest.description:
The migration operation's body.

`to` travels again rather than being read out of the token: the token is
opaque to the caller, and an operation that took the destination *only* from
its own ledger would give a caller no way to say what it thought it was
doing — so a mismatch would be undetectable instead of a 400.

from.description:
The owner the operation found. On a retry after the move already
committed this is already the destination.

terminated_sessions.description:
The sessions this call closed. Empty on a retry, and empty when the
workspace was already where it was being sent.

sessions_closed.description: Whether the terminals closed. `false` means nothing after it ran.

mutation_applied.description:
Whether the Store reassignment committed. `false` with
`sessions_closed: true` is the partial failure, and the retry is the
same request with a fresh confirmation.

projects_rescoped.description:
**The projects whose typed scope now names the new owner**, or `None`
when the session host could not be asked.

Three-valued on purpose, and the third value is the one that matters.
`Some([])` is "the host was asked and had nothing to repair" — the
ordinary answer for a workspace with no projects, and for a retry.
`None` is "nobody has repaired them yet": the move committed, and until
a repair lands those projects name a profile that no longer owns the
workspace, so the terminal draws them in its missing-workspace area
rather than lying about where they live. Sending the same request again
is what repairs them.

A repair that could not run is deliberately *not* a failed migration.
The workspace has moved, the fact is published, and every other reader
is right; treating an unreachable session host as a failure would
invite a caller to retry the whole operation as though nothing had
happened.

WorkspaceMigrationOutcome.description:
What the migration actually did, in the order it did it.

The same shape whether it succeeded, for [`WorkspaceLifecycleOutcome`]'s
reason: a caller reporting a partial failure needs the body it would have
read on success.

EventBatch.description:
`POST /v1/events` — publish a batch. Order is preserved; each event is
accepted, deduplicated or rejected on its own.

version.description:
The `(name, version)` pair identifies the payload shape. Bumped per
event name on breaking change only; additive attrs do not bump it, and
a pair is never reused with a different meaning.

occurred_at_ms.description: Wall clock, epoch ms UTC. Display and bucketing ONLY — never ordering.

correlation_id.description:
The chain root. `None` means this event is its own root — readers use
[`Envelope::chain_root`], never the raw field.

Envelope.description: One event on the local bus.

EventName.description:
A registry-validated dotted event name, e.g. `document.created`.

Construct literals through [`crate::event_name!`], which fails the *build*
on a name missing from the registry; a runtime-built name is refused by
[`crate::validate`] at the boundary instead.

id.description:
The actor's durable identity, when it has one a rule could name.
A person at this profile usually has none; an agent or device does.

token.description:
A registered name token — an agent's name, a system component
(`store`, `importer`, `sync`). Lowercase `[a-z0-9_-]`, never prose.

device_id.description:
This installation, when the emitter knows it. Local-only: stripped at
the telemetry boundary.

session_id.description:
The application run that emitted it. Ephemeral by construction, so it
is the one origin field a telemetry event may carry.

Scope.description:
Where in the data model the event applies. The profile is usually implicit
(the journal is profile-local today); it is carried so a multi-profile
device can tell its own events apart.

id.description: The store's id for it, as the store spells it.

version.description: The store sequence of the state referred to, when known.

Subject.description:
What the event is about, when it is about one thing. A reference, never
content: the consumer fetches the thing through the store.

SubjectKind.description:
Closed on purpose: a new subject kind is an additive, reviewed change,
not a string somebody invents at a call site.

`Task` is one task, by the `task:<workspace>:<document>:<node>` spelling
[`Subject::task`] writes. A *node* is the task (ADR-272); the kind exists
because addressing that node as a task is a different question from
addressing it as content, and the two must not answer each other.

oneOf.description:
A reference (`LocalReference` class): valid on the local bus, dropped
mechanically at the telemetry boundary. (`RefId` is only the schema's
name for it — serde carries the bare uuid string.)
Epoch milliseconds UTC.
A value from the key's declared closed vocabulary.

A signed quantity — a UTC offset, a delta. `Count` for anything that
cannot be negative.

A dotted numeric version — `10.0.26200`. Its own kind rather than a
token because a version has no closed vocabulary, and rather than a
free string because the boundary enforces digits and dots only: it is
structurally incapable of carrying content.
A client-side bucketed numeric — see [`crate::bucket`].

AttrValue.description:
A typed attribute value. **There is deliberately no free-string variant**:
content cannot be smuggled through an attribute by construction. A string
only exists as [`AttrValue::Token`], whose values come from the vocabulary
the registry declares for that key.

last_seq.description:
The journal's latest sequence after this batch — a subscriber's
starting cursor.

AppendReceipt.description:
What `POST /v1/events` answers. Duplicates are success — that is what
makes retrying under the same `event_id` idempotent.

index.description: Index into the batch as sent.

code.description:
A stable ASCII code, never prose (`unknown_event`, `undeclared_attr`,
`events_disabled`, …).

message.description: Untranslated developer text. Not for people.

RejectedEvent.description: One refused event, by position and stable code (`Violation::code`).

next_after.description:
Pass this back as `after` to continue; equal to the request's `after`
when the page is empty.

EventPage.description: `GET /v1/events` — one page of the journal after a cursor.

seq.description: The delivery cursor. Totally ordered per journal, never reused.

recorded_at_ms.description:
The journal's own clock at append — `recorded - occurred` is the
delivery latency the debug flag prints.

StoredEvent.description: One journaled event: the envelope plus what only the journal knows.

retention_days.description:
**How far back this answer can possibly reach.** Activity is
device-local and the journal keeps nothing beyond this window, so an
empty page has two readings — nothing happened, or it happened longer
ago than this — and a surface can only say the honest one if it is told
the number. It is carried on every page rather than only on an empty
one, because a *full* page is equally horizonless without it.

ActivityPage.description:
`GET /v1/events/activity` — one bounded page of one subject's activity.

Paged exactly like [`EventPage`]: a `seq` cursor, oldest first, `next_after`
to continue, and `next_after` equal to the request's `after` when the page
is empty. One cursor convention across the whole journal is what keeps a
page from being silently skipped.

seq.description:
The journal position. The page cursor, and the **only** ordering: two
entries are compared by this and never by `occurred_at_ms`.

occurred_at_ms.description:
Wall clock, epoch ms UTC. **Display only** — clocks skew and devices
sleep, so a surface prints this and orders by `seq`.

actor.description: Who acted, as a kind: a person, an agent, or a part of the system.

actor_token.description:
The actor's registered name token when it has one — an agent's name, a
system component (`store`, `importer`). Lowercase and from a closed
vocabulary, never prose, and absent for a person at this profile.

correlation_id.description:
**The causal group.** A cascade — completing a parent completes every
task under it — is a set of events sharing one of these, not one event
with a count, so a pane folds a group into one line by this key. It is
[`Envelope::chain_root`] already resolved: an event that started its own
chain reports its own id, so this is never absent and a reader never
has to know the `None`-means-self rule.

attrs.description:
The event's declared attributes, whole — see the type doc for why that
cannot be content.

ActivityEntry.description:
One line of a subject's activity — **a projection of an envelope, not the
envelope.**

A pane asking "what happened to this task" wants what happened, when, who
did it and which lines belong to one gesture. It does not want the device
id, the profile id, the emitting session, the payload version or the
journal's own append clock, all of which a [`StoredEvent`] carries. Sending
the whole envelope would mean handing a rendering surface a device identity
it has no use for, and every later field added to the envelope with it — so
the row is enumerated here and the envelope stays the journal's shape.

**No content, structurally.** The only free-form thing an envelope holds is
its attributes, and [`AttrValue`] has no free-string variant: a value is a
reference, a time, a count, a flag, or a token from the vocabulary the
registry declared for that key. So passing the map through whole cannot leak
a title, a due date, a tag name or a line of text, and the pane gets the
tokens it actually needs — `reason` on a lifecycle event, `change` and
`temporal_kind` on a Due change, `child` on a structural one — without this
type learning a field per event.

mode.description:
Raw remains the compatibility default. Managed creation is accepted
only for a profile whose provider passes the rooted host handshake.

working_directory.description: An absolute local path. The Agent-owned host validates it at spawn.

ProviderKind.description: Provider category, never a provider-native identity.

project_id.description:
The project this session was placed in, if any. Absent from a peer
that predates projects, which is why it defaults rather than being
required; absent for a session nobody placed, which the tree draws
under its virtual Unassigned bucket rather than a persisted project.

handover.description:
Protocol v14. Where a controller handover stands. `Idle` from a peer
that predates handovers, which is the truth on a host that has none.

model.description:
Protocol v14. The model the session asked for and the one last
reported, for a managed session whose adapter can say. `None` from a
raw session, an older peer, or an adapter that reports neither.

origin.description:
Protocol v16. What created this session. `Manual` from a peer that
predates origins, which is the truth for every session a window made.
A chat's session is never drawn by a window, a tray or a flyout: its
chat is its view.

SessionFailure.description: A content-free developer diagnostic. UI maps `code` to localized copy.

ErrorCode.description: Stable error token; unknown values remain errors.

oneOf.description: Someone asked while a controller was held; the holder has been told.

The holder released its lease for the handover; the next attach takes
it.
The lease was granted after a release: a person holds the session.
The person gave the lease back, or lost it; the next attach reclaims.

HandoverState.description:
Where a controller handover stands.

Release, not preemption: nothing takes a lease from its holder. The
holder is asked, releases at a boundary of its choosing, the requester
attaches, and gives it back the same way. Each step is a state a reader
can see and an event a subscriber receives.

ModelIdentity.description:
The model a session asked for and the model the provider says it used.

They differ — a provider may reroute — and a provider may say nothing,
which is an explicit `None` rather than a copy of the request. Pricing
needs the reported one; a comparison across runs needs both.

ModelName.description:
A provider's model name, as the provider spells it.

Bounded and printable, and otherwise opaque: Koru compares it, stores it
beside a run's economics and prices it at display, but never interprets
it. It is not an event attribute — `AttrValue` has no free string, and
the bus carries an `Id` reference to retained metadata instead (§17.3).

SessionOrigin.description:
What created a session. Defaulted to `Manual` on every peer that
predates it, which is the truth: before v16 only windows created
sessions without a delegation launch.

resume.description:
Independent cursors captured atomically with `snapshot`. After any
stream gap, reconnect using both values; neither can be derived from the
render snapshot's own sequence.

sequence.description: Last event incorporated in this bounded snapshot.

index.description: Stable retained-row coordinate, never an emulator-relative line index.

wrapped_to_next.description: The terminal's logical line continues directly into the next grid row.

text.description: One grapheme or an empty string for a wide-cell continuation.

mouse_reporting.description:
Compatibility summary retained for existing clients. New input paths
use `mouse_tracking` and `mouse_encoding` below.

after_event.description:
Last event sequence the caller consumed. Event and raw-output counters
are independent and therefore cannot share one cursor.

after_output.description: Last raw-output sequence the caller consumed.

data_base64.description: Base64-encoded process bytes. Access logs never record this value.

Base64-encoded image bytes. Media type and extension are detected from
the decoded bytes; the public caller supplies neither a path nor a name.

message.description: Content-free developer detail. Never a path, filename, or input value.

attachment_ids.description: Ordered by the caller composing this logical input.

oneOf.description:
Protocol v14. The controller handover moved: someone asked, the holder
released, the lease was taken, or it was given back. A new tag, so a
host never sends it to a peer that negotiated less than v14.

SessionEvent.description:
Lifecycle and low-volume facts for one session. Render content has its own
bounded [`crate::RenderUpdate`] stream.

RawOutputChunk.description:
One bounded chunk for an explicitly authorized non-visual output
subscription. Render subscribers consume `RenderUpdate` instead.

post.summary: A delegated run's MCP endpoint (Streamable HTTP, stateless)
post.description: The endpoint a delegated provider is handed. Authenticated by the run's own bearer (issued through POST /v1/artifacts/authorities), resolved against the durable authority record on every call — never by a gateway session bearer. One JSON-RPC message per POST, answered as application/json; a notification is 202; GET and DELETE are 405. Exactly six tools: create, create_version, get, read, search, attach_to_run. Their definitions, as tools/list returns them, are in x-mcp-tools.

x-mcp-tools.title: Register a new result
x-mcp-tools.description: Register a file you wrote under your .artifacts/<RunId>/ folder as a new artifact in the run's workspace. `path` is relative to that folder (or absolute and inside it); `title` is what a person will call the result. A second call with the same path and the same bytes returns the same version; the same path with new bytes registers the next version of the same artifact.
